Cognitive demands are moderate: workers follow established practices and make local judgments about ripeness, damage, and handling, but typically not complex planning. Social/emotional requirements are generally low, though coordination and supervision matter. Automation is most feasible for grading/sorting/packing, some pesticide/fertilizer application, and irrigation monitoring; human labor remains critical for delicate harvesting, pruning, and varied field tasks where dexterity and adaptability are needed, especially given safety and regulatory accountability around chemicals and food handling.

Title: Farmworkers, Farm, Ranch, and Aquacultural Animals
rationale: Many daily tasks (feeding schedules, watering, recordkeeping, basic health checks) are routine and can be standardized, making them amenable to automation/AI-assisted monitoring and workflow tools. However, the work is highly physical and occurs in variable outdoor/animal environments, requiring dexterity, mobility, and safe handling that remain difficult for robots at scale. Judgment is needed for detecting illness/injury, assisting births, and administering medications, with meaningful animal welfare and biosecurity consequences, which raises accountability and limits full automation. Social/emotional demands are moderate (animal handling and coordination with supervisors/vets), but not the primary barrier. Overall, AI can significantly augment (sensing, alerts, records, scheduling), while full replacement is constrained mainly by physical embodiment and high-variance edge cases.

Title: Agricultural Workers, All Other
rationale: This catch-all agricultural worker category typically involves routine, repeatable tasks (planting, harvesting support, sorting, basic equipment operation) that can be partially standardized and measured, making some work amenable to automation. However, the work is often highly physical and performed in variable outdoor conditions, which slows full automation and keeps human labor important where dexterity and adaptability are needed. Cognitive demands are usually moderate-to-low, with situational judgment (weather, crop condition, equipment issues) but limited deep analytical reasoning. Social/emotional requirements are generally modest, though coordination and safety communication matter. Automation is most feasible for repetitive field operations, monitoring, and sorting via robotics/vision systems, while edge cases, mixed tasks, and unstructured environments remain human-critical.

Title: Fishing and Hunting Workers
rationale: Fishing and hunting work includes some standardized, repeatable procedures (setting gear, following seasons/quotas, handling catch), but conditions vary widely by weather, terrain, species behavior, and local regulations. The job is highly physical and environment-dependent, requiring on-site presence, manual handling of equipment and animals, and safe operation on vessels or in the field, which strongly limits full automation. Cognitive demands are moderate: workers must interpret changing conditions, locate targets, and make real-time safety and compliance judgments. Social/emotional demands are usually limited, though coordination with crew and adherence to community/regulatory expectations matter. Automation is most feasible for sensing/locating (sonar, drones), route planning, catch monitoring, and some mechanized hauling/processing; human-critical elements include field safety, ethical/legal judgment, and robust physical work in unstructured environments.

Title: Forest and Conservation Workers
rationale: Many tasks (planting, seedling transport, basic pest control, erosion-control structure building) follow standard procedures and can be partially codified, but conditions vary by terrain, weather, and site-specific ecology. The work is highly physical and outdoors, requiring mobility, tool use, and adaptation to uneven, cluttered environments—areas where robotics is still costly and less reliable, limiting full automation. Cognitive demands are moderate: workers must recognize issues (pests/disease signs, site hazards) and apply protocols, often under supervision. Social/emotional requirements are generally low to moderate, mostly coordination and safety communication rather than deep client-facing trust work. AI can augment planning, monitoring, and documentation (e.g., pest detection from imagery, work routing, compliance checklists), while on-the-ground manual labor and safety-critical judgment in dynamic field conditions remain human-critical.

Title: Fallers
rationale: Tree felling has well-known techniques and safety procedures, but each tree and site presents variable conditions (lean, rot, wind, terrain, nearby assets) that reduce full standardization. The work is highly physical and requires real-world dexterity with chainsaws/axes and precise positioning, making it difficult to automate without advanced field robotics. Cognitive demands are moderate-to-high due to continuous hazard assessment and selecting cuts to control fall direction under uncertainty. Social/emotional demands are limited, though coordination and safety communication with a crew can matter. Errors can be severe (injury, property/environmental damage), so accountability and safety constraints limit autonomous deployment; AI is more likely to augment via planning, risk assessment, and training rather than replace the worker end-to-end.

Title: Logging Equipment Operators
rationale: Logging equipment operation involves repeatable machine-control routines (skidding, loading, stacking) that can be partially standardized, but conditions vary widely by terrain, weather, tree species, and site constraints. The work is highly physically embodied and safety-critical, requiring real-time perception and control in unstructured outdoor environments, which limits full automation despite advances in autonomy and machine vision. Cognitive demands include situational judgment (stability, line-of-fire hazards, load dynamics) and adapting plans as conditions change. Social/emotional requirements are moderate-low, mostly coordination with crew and adherence to safety protocols rather than deep interpersonal work. Automation is most feasible for assistive features (collision avoidance, stability monitoring, semi-autonomous grapple/boom control, optimized routing and stacking) and for controlled tasks like chipping or repetitive loading, while felling decisions, complex maneuvering, and accountability for safety remain human-critical.

Title: Log Graders and Scalers
rationale: Log grading/scaling follows established grading rules and measurement standards, making much of the evaluation relatively codifiable and suitable for computer vision and sensor-based automation. However, real-world variability (species differences, irregular shapes, dirt/ice, lighting, partial occlusion, and ambiguous defects) still requires contextual judgment and experience, especially when quality/value is borderline. The work is physically situated in yards and decks and often involves handling, positioning, and safely accessing logs, which raises the physical embodiment barrier for full automation without robust robotics. Social demands are limited, but decisions affect pricing, inventory, and downstream processing, so errors can be costly and may require accountable human oversight. Highest automation potential is in measurement (volume/diameter/length) and defect detection/recordkeeping; human-critical elements include safety, edge-case grading calls, and accountability in disputes.

Title: Logging Workers, All Other
rationale: Logging workers perform many repeatable, procedure-driven tasks (e.g., bucking, limbing, rigging, equipment support), but conditions vary widely by terrain, weather, and timber characteristics, limiting full standardization. The work is highly physical and outdoors, requiring mobility, dexterity, and real-time adaptation around heavy machinery and unstable environments, which strongly constrains near-term automation. Cognitive demands are moderate: workers must assess hazards, coordinate sequences, and troubleshoot equipment/process issues on site. Stakes are high due to safety risks and potential environmental/regulatory consequences, increasing the need for human oversight and accountability. Automation is most feasible via mechanized harvesters, remote/assisted equipment operation, sensors, mapping, and planning/dispatch; fully replacing on-the-ground roles is harder because of physical variability and safety-critical judgment.

Social coordination with crews, customers, inspectors, and subcontractors remains important, and accountability is relatively high due to electrical/fire safety, code compliance, and liability—favoring human oversight even when AI assists.

Title: Boilermakers
rationale: Boilermaking includes many standardized, blueprint-driven tasks (layout, alignment, assembly, inspection checklists) that are partially codifiable and can be augmented by digital tools, sensors, and computer vision. However, the work is highly physical and site-specific, requiring heavy-material handling, precise fitting, welding/fastening, and safe work in constrained industrial environments—areas where general-purpose robotics remains limited. Cognitive demands are moderate: interpreting drawings, diagnosing fit-up and equipment issues, and adapting to field conditions and tolerances. Stakes are high due to pressure-vessel safety, regulatory compliance, and liability, which favors human oversight and sign-off even when AI assists with measurement, documentation, and defect detection. The most automatable components are planning, blueprint interpretation support, measurement/QA capture, predictive maintenance analytics, and documentation; the least automatable are on-site manipulation, complex repairs, and safety-critical judgment in dynamic conditions.

Title: Brickmasons and Blockmasons
rationale: Brickmasons and blockmasons perform work with many standardized methods (mixing mortar, laying courses, checking plumb/level), but real-world variability in site conditions, materials, and tolerances reduces full codifiability. The job is highly physical and requires dexterity, positioning, and continuous adjustment to uneven substrates and environmental factors, which makes automation difficult without advanced robotics. Cognitive demands are moderate: reading plans, sequencing work, and troubleshooting fit/finish issues, but much of the workflow is repeatable. Social demands are present but limited, mainly coordination with crews, supervisors, and inspectors. Automation is most plausible for augmentation (layout assistance, measurement/QA via vision, robotic placement in controlled settings like factories) rather than broad on-site replacement, with humans remaining critical for complex installs, repairs, and accountability for structural quality and safety.

Title: Stonemasons
rationale: Stonemasonry involves some standardized procedures (measuring, cutting, setting, mortaring, leveling), but real-world variability in stone, site conditions, and tolerances reduces full codifiability. The work is highly physical and requires dexterous manipulation of heavy, irregular materials, making end-to-end automation difficult without advanced robotics and jobsite integration. Cognitive demands are moderate: interpreting plans, ensuring alignment/drainage, and adapting to unexpected fit and substrate issues. Social/emotional requirements are typically limited to coordination with crews and clients, though communication about aesthetics and constraints matters. Many subtasks can be augmented by AI (estimating quantities, layout optimization, CAD-to-cut lists, vision-based QC), but on-site placement, finishing, and safety-critical judgment remain human-critical.

Title: Carpenters
rationale: Carpentry includes many standardized, codifiable tasks (measuring, cutting lists, framing patterns, installation sequences) that can be partially automated via CAD/CAM, prefabrication, and AI-assisted estimating and layout. Moderate cognitive complexity is needed for interpreting plans, resolving clashes, ensuring level/plumb/square, and troubleshooting unforeseen constraints. Social interaction is present but typically limited to coordination with clients, inspectors, and other trades rather than deep counseling or negotiation. Accountability is meaningful because errors can create safety/structural issues and code violations, so human oversight and sign-off remain critical even as planning, documentation, and some fabrication steps become more automated.

Title: Carpet Installers
rationale: Carpet installation follows fairly standardized steps (measuring, cutting, stretching, seaming, trimming), making planning and estimation partially codifiable, but real-world variability in rooms and subfloors reduces full predictability. Cognitive demands are moderate: installers must diagnose fit issues, align patterns, and manage seams and transitions, but most decisions are procedural rather than deeply analytical. Social interaction is present (customer coordination, explaining options, handling complaints) but typically not highly therapeutic or negotiation-heavy. Errors can be costly (material waste, rework, damage to property), so accountability is meaningful; AI can assist with measurement, layout optimization, quoting, and quality-check guidance, while humans remain critical for on-site execution and final judgment.

Title: Commercial Pilots
rationale: Commercial piloting includes many standardized, procedure-driven tasks (checklists, navigation, communications, normal operations) that are amenable to automation and AI augmentation, but real-world variability limits full codification. Social/emotional demands are moderate (ATC coordination, passenger/client interaction) but not the core differentiator. Title: Air Traffic Controllers
rationale: Air traffic control is highly procedural and data-driven (clear separation minima, phraseology, checklists), making many monitoring, alerting, and coordination sub-tasks amenable to automation. Physical embodiment is low because the job is primarily digital/communications-based, but social/communication skill remains important for clear, calm coordination with pilots and adjacent sectors. Stakes are extremely high with strong regulatory accountability, which limits full automation and favors decision-support systems (conflict detection, sequencing, routing suggestions) with human controllers retaining final authority. Overall, significant augmentation is feasible, but end-to-end automation is constrained by safety certification, rare edge cases, and accountability requirements.

Title: Airfield Operations Specialists
rationale: Airfield Operations Specialists perform many standardized, checklist-driven tasks (safety procedures, recordkeeping, dispatch coordination) that are amenable to software automation and AI decision support. However, the role also requires high contextual judgment under time pressure (weather changes, runway conditions, irregular operations) and tight integration with real-time operational constraints, which limits full automation. Physical presence is often needed for airfield inspections, verifying hazards/FOD, and coordinating on-site responses, though sensing/monitoring can reduce some of this. Communication and coordination with ATC, maintenance, and flight crews is central and can be augmented (alerts, summaries, routing), but trust and shared situational awareness remain human-critical. Because errors can have severe safety consequences and regulatory accountability is high, AI is more likely to be used for monitoring, anomaly detection, and decision support than for autonomous control.

Title: Flight Attendants
rationale: Many routine service elements (announcements, checklists, inventory tracking, meal/beverage ordering, and documentation) are structured and could be heavily augmented by AI. However, the role requires continuous physical presence in a constrained, safety-critical environment, including assisting passengers, operating cabin equipment, and managing real-world contingencies. High social/emotional skill is central for de-escalation, reassurance, and compliance, especially during delays, medical events, and conflicts. Cognitive demands rise sharply in irregular operations and emergencies where rapid situational judgment is needed. Because errors can have severe safety and regulatory consequences and accountability remains with crew, end-to-end automation is unlikely; AI will mainly support training, monitoring, and decision aids rather than replace attendants.

Title: Driver/Sales Workers

Title: Heavy and Tractor-Trailer Truck Drivers
rationale: Long-haul driving has many standardized elements (routes, hours-of-service rules, inspections, logging), making portions of the work codifiable and increasingly sensor/AI-assisted. However, real-world driving still requires robust perception and judgment in edge cases (weather, construction, unpredictable road users), and the job often includes physical tasks like coupling/uncoupling trailers, inspections, fueling, and occasional unloading. Social demands are moderate (dispatch coordination, customers, law enforcement) but typically not highly emotionally nuanced. Title: Light Truck Drivers
rationale: Route execution, pickup/drop-off workflows, scanning, and compliance steps are fairly standardized and measurable, making significant portions amenable to automation/optimization. Social/emotional skill is usually limited to brief customer interactions, though professionalism and conflict handling matter in edge cases. Title: Bus Drivers, School
rationale: Core driving and route adherence are relatively standardized and measurable, making parts of the work (routing, scheduling, compliance checklists, incident reporting) amenable to automation/AI assistance. Social-emotional demands are moderate because drivers must maintain order, communicate with children, and handle conflicts or special needs appropriately. Title: Bus Drivers, Transit and Intercity
rationale: Core driving tasks are partially structured (routes, schedules, fare rules) and increasingly supportable by driver-assist and dispatch/optimization software, but real-world traffic, weather, construction, and passenger behavior add variability and judgment. The work is highly physically embodied and safety-critical, requiring continuous real-time control of a large vehicle and situational awareness in complex environments. Social interaction is moderate: managing passenger questions, conflicts, accessibility needs, and ensuring a safe onboard environment often benefits from human presence. Creativity demands are low, but accountability is high due to public safety, regulatory compliance, and liability. Near-term automation is most feasible for back-office functions (routing, scheduling, fare collection, reporting) and limited autonomy in constrained corridors; full driver replacement is constrained by safety, edge cases, and supervision requirements.

Title: Shuttle Drivers and Chauffeurs
rationale: Core driving and routing tasks are highly standardized (fixed routes, schedules, pickup/drop-off procedures), making portions amenable to automation and dispatch optimization. However, the work is strongly constrained by physical-world operation of a vehicle in dynamic environments, which remains a major barrier outside geofenced or highly controlled settings. Social interaction is moderate: customer service, assisting riders (including medical transport and bereavement contexts), and handling complaints or special needs often require human judgment and empathy. Stakes are meaningful due to passenger safety, regulatory compliance, and liability, which slows full automation even if driver-assist features can reduce workload. Near-term automation is most plausible via advanced driver assistance, telematics, automated scheduling/fare collection, and partial autonomy on predictable routes; fully driverless operation is less reliable across varied conditions and passenger needs.

Title: Taxi Drivers
rationale: Core driving and routing are increasingly codifiable and measurable (navigation, dispatch, pricing), making significant portions amenable to automation. Social skills matter for customer service and conflict de-escalation, but interactions are typically brief and procedural. Accountability is moderate-to-high due to safety, legal liability, and passenger welfare, which slows full automation even as driver-assist and autonomous systems expand.

Title: Motor Vehicle Operators, All Other

Title: Locomotive Engineers
rationale: Locomotive engineering involves many standardized procedures (signals, rules, timetables, braking curves) that are amenable to automation and decision support, especially under well-instrumented rail networks. However, operators must handle irregular situations (equipment faults, weather, track obstructions, work zones, unexpected signal behavior) that require contextual judgment and conservative risk management. The work is partly physical due to on-site presence, cab operations, inspections, and coordination with yard/field staff, though much of the core control task is digital/controls-based. Social/emotional demands are generally limited, but communication and coordination remain important. Stakes are high (safety, hazardous materials, passenger risk, regulatory compliance), which slows full automation and keeps humans critical for accountability and exception handling even as ATO/PTC-like systems automate routine driving.

Title: Railroad Conductors and Yardmasters

Title: Subway and Streetcar Operators
rationale: Operating trains/streetcars follows highly standardized routes, signals, schedules, and safety procedures, making much of the core driving task relatively codifiable and amenable to automation. Title: Rail Transportation Workers, All Other

Title: Sailors and Marine Oilers

Title: Ship Engineers
rationale: Ship engineers’ work includes many standardized procedures (watchstanding, maintenance schedules, checklists, regulatory compliance) that are amenable to software support and partial automation, especially via condition monitoring and predictive maintenance. The role is strongly physical and environment-dependent (inspections, repairs, operating machinery in constrained spaces), which current AI/robotics cannot reliably replace aboard ships. Supervisory coordination is important but typically less emotionally nuanced than counseling/negotiation-heavy roles, making some communication and documentation tasks automatable. High stakes (safety, environmental compliance, propulsion reliability) mean humans remain accountable for decisions, though AI can augment with alerts, diagnostics, and optimized operating parameters.

Title: Bridge and Lock Tenders
rationale: Much of the work follows standardized procedures (opening/closing bridges or operating lock gates, signaling, logging, and safety checks), making it relatively codifiable and amenable to automation. Title: Automotive and Watercraft Service Attendants

Title: Aircraft Service Attendants

Title: Traffic Technicians

Title: Transportation Inspectors

Judgment is needed to interpret ambiguous findings, prioritize risks, and decide when to ground equipment or escalate issues, especially when evidence is incomplete. The most automatable parts are documentation review, anomaly detection from sensor/vision data, report generation, and scheduling; human-critical parts include on-site verification, nuanced defect assessment, and final compliance/safety determinations.

Title: Aviation Inspectors
rationale: Aviation inspection work is heavily guided by federal regulations, checklists, documentation standards, and measurable tolerances, making many components structured and amenable to software automation. The job often requires on-site physical inspection of aircraft and equipment, limiting full automation without advanced robotics, though computer vision, sensors, and digital twins can automate portions of defect detection and trend analysis. Social interaction is moderate (coordination with maintenance, operators, and regulators) but typically less emotionally nuanced than counseling or sales roles. Stakes are high and accountability is significant (safety, compliance, enforcement), so humans are likely to remain in the loop for final determinations even as AI augments evidence gathering, anomaly detection, report drafting, and compliance cross-checking.

Title: Transportation Workers, All Other

Title: Crane and Tower Operators
rationale: Crane and tower operation includes many standardized procedures (load charts, signaling protocols, checklists), making portions of the work codifiable, but real-world variability (wind, blind lifts, site constraints) reduces full predictability.
